title: Great Expectations - Or Not So Great
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona's main teaching emphasizes the importance of releasing expectations and dualistic thinking in meditation, encouraging listeners to focus on being present in each moment rather than striving for a specific state or outcome. By letting go of attachments and preconceptions, we can awaken to life as it truly is, experiencing surprises and growth, and cultivating a deeper understanding of impermanence through the practice of sitting meditation with patience and persistence. This approach allows us to find comfort in our spiritual journey, even when faced with challenges and uncertainties.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating, [unclear: "non-perfect"] dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the tathagata's roots.*
Yeah, a little picture.
A pen to stick in there or something?
How about a key?
Maybe not.
Just hold on, it will be okay.
Welcome to the folks online too.
Great expectations.
Not so great.
A close friend of mine was recently talking with some other friends of 15 years.
A long discussion resulted in them deciding to do a reboot on the relationship of 15 years, wanting to bring more positivity into their lives together.
Are there any relationships that you're in where you'd like to do that?
Boot the relationship.
Consider the challenges to doing that.
Why is it so hard?
Maybe it's because we've established expectations of each other.

This retreat is billed as a Beginner's Mind retreat, which is a reference, of course, to *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind*, a collection of talks by Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, the Japanese priest who seeded this lineage that we're practicing in, in San Francisco.
The aspect of Beginner's Mind that I would like to focus on today is expectations.
So let's look at a few things Shunryu Suzuki had to say on expectations to start.
*We say our practice should be without gaining ideas, without any expectations, even of enlightenment.
This does not mean, however, just to sit without any purpose.*
So sitting meditation is an opportunity to study our mind in a simplified container.
What does it mean to sit without expectations?
What do we expect?
What do we expect just in the moment today, say an hour ago, sitting down?
Expect boredom?
Expect pain?
And so as we're sitting, if we find expectations present, does that mean that we're doing meditation wrong?
Of course not.
That's the point: to sit and notice what's there, and to find that opportunity to let go of creating the conditions for what's arising in the mind.
Shunryu Suzuki also said:
*While you are continuing this practice week after week, year after year, your experience will become deeper and deeper, and your experience will cover everything that you do in your everyday life.
The most important thing is to forget all gaining ideas, all dualistic ideas.
In other words, just practice zazen in a certain posture.
Do not think about anything.
Just remain on your cushion without expecting anything.
Then eventually you will resume your own true nature.
That is to say, your own true nature resumes itself.*
The true self is not the self I build, the self that makes expectations about who I should be or how people should treat me.
I recognized this recently when I was doing laundry.
I walked into the laundry room, which is also the room where the cat food is stored, and the cat looked up at me and said, "Feed me!"
I said, "No, no, it's not time to eat yet."
The cat said, "Feed me!"
Well, nobody talks to me that way.
Okay, this feels like it's more about me than it is about you.
About protecting that self.
Another quote from Suzuki Roshi:
*Extraordinary progress.
Even though you try very hard, the progress you make is always little by little.
This is the Soto way of practice.
We can say either that we make progress little by little or that we do not even expect to make progress.
Just to be sincere and make our full effort in each moment is enough.
There is no nirvana outside of our practice.*
*Just to be sincere and make our full effort in each moment is enough.
There is no nirvana outside of our practice.*
In the question and answer group, we're reviewing the difference between the two major current Japanese Zen lineages, Soto and Rinzai.
Rinzai focuses more on koans, this being a Soto group, and Rinzai also looks more at sudden changes.
Suzuki Roshi here is really pointing at this difference: our way is little by little, very subtle changes.
And then that bit about there is nirvana outside of our practice.
Outside of being fully present.
But being fully present is nirvana.
And of course, our practice becomes our whole life, and our whole life becomes our practice.
So next, in looking at expectations, we'll start with [unclear: "Thales'"] four steps to sitting meditation.
Right back to the very beginning.
Sitting meditation, step one: we sit with good posture.
Step two: we bring our attention to what's present, possibly to our breath or some other focal point.
Step three: we notice that our attention is no longer at that focal point.
And step four: we come back.
And just again and again and again, coming back.
That returning is the practice.

When we notice that we are no longer with that focal point, one practice that we have received from other non-Zen lineages of Buddhism, older lineages, Vipassana, for example, insight meditation, is the practice of naming.
Not just noticing that I'm no longer present, but giving a quick, brief name to what it is that took me aside.
It might be as simple as "thinking."
Thinking it as "thinking about what I'm going to say to my colleague tomorrow when I confront him" is way too detailed.
But maybe "fixing," "worrying," or "expecting."
So I'll invite you today, if you feel like this might be fruitful for you, in the practice of naming what has taken you off to the side, maybe to pay particular attention to expecting.
In talking about the different variants of Buddhism, one teaching is that there are three seals of Buddhism that any variant will have as part of them.
One of them is non-self.
The concept of non-self is challenging to us and can be a source of years of study, and a source that maybe you never feel comfortable with.
The second seal is the cessation of suffering.
That one's not quite so challenging, usually.
Probably you've got some feeling for the cessation of suffering as a possibility, and distress being in our lives.
Or you wouldn't be here.
Probably.
Maybe not.
That takes some study.
And the third seal is impermanence.
It seems impermanence is maybe less difficult to grasp, at least on an initial level, without getting into radical impermanence.
We understand nobody expects that nothing's going to change.
We all know that it's not permanent, that things are constantly in flux.
And yet we don't act that way.
We don't act like we know that things are going to change.
For example, in noticing planning while sitting: planning is expecting that this is the situation I'm going to be in in the future.
Maybe we have good reason to believe that we're going to be at work on Monday.
But it is still an expectation and an opportunity to let go.
As we're sitting there in meditation, the empty mind is looking for something to fill itself with.
And maybe sometimes you'll notice recalling conflict that you've had with someone.

Another opportunity to look at expectation, and to remember that when we're in conflict with someone, we are probably mistaken in our expectations about what their perspective and their motivation are.
So we've identified these expectations.
Now, how do we let them go?
Natalie Goldberg at Upaya Zen Center teaches haiku as Zen practice because it contains a leap, usually.

It contains a little sensation of space, these Japanese poem forms that set up a context and then move us out of our expectations, create some space that moves us out of what we expect ourselves to be.
Or: on Friday, my boss came to work in a beautiful new car.
It was really a sweet model and I complimented him on it.
And he was straight with me.
He said, well, if you work hard, set goals, you'll be determined and put in long hours, that he could get an even better car next year.
So maybe that joke wasn't funny.
But the ones that are funny trigger something in us because they take us out of our expectations.
Here's a reading from *The Hidden Lamp*.
*Master Lang Wei Wei Ju had a woman disciple who came to him for instruction.
The master told her to examine the saying, "Let it be."
He said that if she faithfully used this sentence as a scythe, she would cut down illusions and reap enlightenment.
The woman followed his instructions faithfully.
One day her house burned down and she said, "Let it be."
Another day her son fell into the water, and when a bystander ran to tell her, she answered, "Let it be."
One day she started to make fried cakes for dinner as her husband lit the fire.
She prepared the batter and heated the oil and then poured a spoonful of batter onto the hot oil.
When she heard the sizzling sound, she was immediately enlightened.
She threw the pan to the ground and jumped up and down, clapping her hands and then laughing.
Her husband shouted at her, "What are you doing?
Have you gone mad?"
And she answered, "Let it be."
Then she went to Wei Ju and he confirmed that she had indeed harvested the holy fruit.*
Tamara Mioho-Gabrish reflects on this koan.
She says:
*At first glance this phrase might look like the perfect excuse to do nothing, or a justification for complacency.
Don't be misled.
Letting things be doesn't mean that we cease functioning, stop thinking or get rid of the self once and for all, as most of us erroneously seem to hope.
In fact, it is quite the opposite.
It is like awakening from a stupor to find everything is very much alive and buzzing.
Let it be, and in that moment our attachment to self can fall away, and an appreciation for this life as the life of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha as one mind can't help but express itself.
A simple grain of rice left in the rice cooker is as valuable as the nugget of gold.*
Maybe when her home burned down this disciple found herself looking forward to a fresh start.
Expectations.
Maybe her son was an enthusiastic swimmer who was diving into the water every free moment he had.
Maybe seeing her fried batter fly through the air and land on the floor was thrilling.
Who knows?
When we actively let things be, surprises can happen.
Letting go of expectations when my wife Diane died was one thing I did right.
I listened to friends and counselors who told me grief expresses itself differently for everyone.
Everyone has their own path of grief, and it differs for anyone from one moment to another.
Letting go of expectations about how the process should be allowed me to open up to my passions and to directly witness the transcendental beauty that our love was, to experience that in new ways.
We fear letting go of expectations.
When we manage to let go of fears and expectations, that leaves us facing emptiness.
Teacher Jane Schneider says:
*The one thing we can do for comfort about the state of the world and the state of our lives is mainly to take comfort in our spiritual friends.
Because they're all going through the same things right now.
And their delusions are falling too.
And we're starting to grow weeds we hadn't actually planned on, so we can get together.
We can laugh about our shared delusions.
We can take comfort that each of us grows through these delusions even before they fall off.
After we take comfort in our friends, we turn our attention to others whose delusions are also falling to the ground.
It's something just about delusions.
That everybody in the world is experiencing them too.
And we can't keep them.*
Last week Tim quoted Buddhist instructions for correcting people.
One of those instructions was to ask, "Is the heart of goodwill free from malice established in me towards my fellow wayfarers in the holy life?"
I love that language.
My fellow wayfarers in the holy life.
It highlights the adventure that this is.
This practice of sitting silently doing nothing is adventurous.
Letting go of expectations doesn't mean shouting them down.
Jane Schneider again said:
*The first thing we have to do is stop justifying our delusions.
And when they're ready to fall away, we let them fall away.*
Have you experienced sitting meditation thinking that you were relaxed, and then realizing that there are actually some muscles that you're holding really tensely?
And it's like, oh.
And drop the shoulders, or oh, and the legs fall back.
Know what I'm talking about?
Have you noticed my mental habits are the same way?
I work at letting go.
I think I've let go.
Okay, that's good, I've let go.
Oh, I haven't.
And then we can relax.
Sometimes because we've noticed, we can actively let go.
Sometimes we're not sure why it lets go.
There was one day at Samish last year where I had a thought that kept arising.
I would sit with it, just knowing what was present.
Notice this thought arising, and then let it go and come back to the breath.
And 15 seconds later, oh, this thought is here again.
Let it go.
With patience and persistence, starting from the beginning of that period toward the end of that period, about 25 minutes.
So I kept, every 15 seconds, 15 goes into 64 times, 25 minutes.
So about 100 times.
Oh, return to the breath.
And then all of a sudden, you know what happened?
It didn't come back.
The expectation was there.
But sometimes it just doesn't come back.
Sometimes impermanence just arises.
So, fellow wayfarers in the holy life, maybe take note of your expectations today and name them as you're meditating.
See if you can stop creating the conditions that support them.
If you can, let them go.
When they're ready to fall away, they will.
And I will practice the same.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.*
*Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
